title: Redesigning healthcare for healthier women and families
gist: The piece argues that value-based care has stalled and women's health is the clearest example of the spend-outcome gap: the US spent $5.7 trillion (18.4% of GDP) on healthcare in 2025, yet preterm births stay at 10.4% and one in three US counties is a maternity care desert. It proposes three design shifts (prevention by default, outcome-based payment, curated care navigation), uses Progyny's fertility-benefit results as the proof case, and positions employers, which cover 165.6 million Americans under 65, as the lever for capturing a WEF/McKinsey-estimated $1 trillion a year economic prize by 2040.

themes.theme: US health spend vs. stalled maternal outcomes

insights.claim: US healthcare spending reached $5.7 trillion in 2025, equal to 18.4% of GDP and a third straight year of growth above 7%, yet core maternal outcomes are not improving.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Healthcare cost growth running above 7% for three years keeps pressure on employers and payers to buy cost-containment and outcome-based vendors.
insights.locator: Introduction: value-based care 20 years on

insights.claim: According to March of Dimes' 2025 report card, hypertension among pregnant patients in the US rose 6%, diabetes rose 8%, and the preterm birth rate stayed at 10.4%, earning a D+ grade for the fourth consecutive year.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Rising pregnancy comorbidities point to growing demand for high-risk obstetric, cardiometabolic and maternal-monitoring services and higher per-birth claims costs.
insights.locator: Few categories highlight the gap between spending and outcomes

insights.claim: The World Health Organization reports that the world is off track on every health-related UN Sustainable Development Goal, with maternal mortality nearly three times the 2030 target.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Missed global maternal-health targets make the area a likely focus for development finance and impact-investing capital.
insights.locator: Yet progress on many of the most critical outcomes has stalled

insights.claim: The authors attribute stalled outcomes to deliberate system design: healthcare is still built to react after people become sick and still rewards visit volume over outcomes, the accumulated result of choices about what is invested in, measured and left to chance.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Framing this as a design choice rather than a funding gap supports business models that re-architect payment incentives, not just add spending.
insights.quote: It's the accumulation of choices — about what we invest, what we measure, and what we leave to chance.
insights.locator: What's preventing progress?

themes.theme: Access gaps even under universal coverage

insights.claim: Having insurance coverage does not guarantee timely care: in England, where coverage is universal, more than 550,000 women are waiting for gynaecological care, with the longest waits in the most deprived communities.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Long public-system waiting lists create openings for private women's-health clinics and outsourcing in the UK.
insights.quote: Offering benefit coverage is not the same as ensuring timely, appropriate care before problems escalate.
insights.locator: Why access is the gateway to value in health

insights.claim: One in three US counties is a maternity care desert, leaving 5.8 million women without full access to maternity care.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Geographic gaps in maternity care support demand for virtual maternity care, remote monitoring and rural obstetric capacity.
insights.locator: Why access is the gateway to value in health

insights.claim: Across OECD countries the average age of mothers at childbirth is now 31.1, up two to five years since 1970, which makes timely access to fertility care and wider women's health support more important.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Later childbearing is a long-term demand driver for fertility services, egg freezing and fertility benefits.
insights.locator: Women are also building families later

insights.claim: The World Economic Forum and McKinsey Health Institute estimate that women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health than men despite living longer, and that closing this gap could add at least $1 trillion a year to the global economy by 2040.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The $1T/yr figure is the headline total-addressable-market number that women's-health investors and policymakers are likely to cite.
insights.locator: The global consequences of inadequate women's health access

themes.theme: Prevention as default: the PMOS case

insights.claim: A 2026 World Economic Forum/McKinsey report estimates that earlier preventive pathways in women's health could give women 2.5 more days of healthy life a year, avert 70,000 adverse medical events in the US alone, and deliver an estimated 3-6x return on investment.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A cited 3-6x ROI is the kind of number employers and payers need before funding upstream screening and education programs.
insights.locator: Shift 1: Make prevention the default

insights.claim: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, until recently called PCOS) is often undiagnosed, affects up to 13% of reproductive-aged women worldwide, raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and endometrial cancer, and is linked to an estimated $8 billion a year in US healthcare costs.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A large, under-diagnosed metabolic condition is an obvious target for diagnostics and cardiometabolic therapeutics that focus on women.
insights.locator: Shift 1: Make prevention the default

insights.claim: Fertility-care consultations, such as a visit about egg freezing, can serve as a point for detecting undiagnosed conditions like PMOS, because women's health is a continuous journey across life stages rather than a series of episodes.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Fertility benefit platforms could grow into broader lifecycle women's-health platforms, which would increase revenue per member.
insights.quote: One conversation at the right time can change a long-term trajectory of care.
insights.locator: Consider the case of a patient who came in to discuss egg freezing

insights.claim: Progyny and other stakeholders in the Women's Health Investment Consortium are working to move investment upstream by tackling the evidence, financing and commercialization barriers that keep earlier detection and prevention from reaching women at scale.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Watch the consortium for signs that capital is flowing into early-detection women's-health ventures.
insights.locator: Through the Women's Health Investment Consortium

insights.claim: Fertility benefit design has long optimized for spend per cycle rather than the likelihood of a healthy baby, even as demand rises and care stays costly for both patients and employers.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Benefit models that pay per cycle are exposed to replacement by managed, outcome-based fertility programs.
insights.locator: Shift 2: Design for outcomes

insights.claim: According to Progyny, nearly half of its members reach their family-building goals through upstream education and guidance alone, without any fertility treatment. No standard utilization report captures this outcome.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: If the figure holds up, it implies structurally lower treatment use per member, which strengthens the case to employers. Treat it as a self-reported vendor figure.
insights.quote: nearly half of Progyny members reach their family-building goals without fertility treatment at all
insights.locator: Shift 2: Design for outcomes

insights.claim: For Progyny members who do have fertility treatment, the reported outcomes are a 23% higher live birth rate, 41% fewer retrievals per live birth and a 61% lower multiples rate, which together produce 30% cost savings for employers. The piece credits this to close alignment with clinics and payment models that reward outcomes.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A 30% employer saving claim, driven largely by lower multiples rates, is the core sales argument for managed fertility benefits. Verify it against independent actuarial data.
insights.locator: For those who do proceed, clinical outcomes drive value

insights.claim: A Cochrane review of continuous labour support, covering trials in 17 countries and more than 15,000 women, found that women with a dedicated birth companion, especially a doula, were 25% less likely to deliver by caesarean.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Evidence that low-cost support lowers high-cost surgical births backs payer coverage of doula services and the maternity-support vendors that provide them.
insights.locator: The pattern holds beyond fertility

insights.claim: In a recent survey nearly 3 in 4 patients said navigating healthcare adds stress to their daily lives. The authors argue that handing patients a provider directory shifts exhausting, unpaid coordination work onto women instead of providing real access.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Supports demand for care-navigation and curated-network platforms as a distinct benefits category.
insights.quote: That's not access; it's exhausting, unpaid work.
insights.locator: Shift 3: Surround women with support

insights.claim: The Massachusetts trial of Lindsay Clancy has drawn attention to postpartum psychosis and to how hard it is to recognize fast-changing symptoms across care settings. The authors stress that the facts are contested, but say the case shows the need for shared information, clear accountability and escalation pathways between providers.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: High-profile postpartum mental-health cases can speed employer and policy interest in perinatal mental-health screening and care coordination.
insights.locator: The stakes of a fragmented system can be stark

insights.claim: Employer-sponsored insurance is the largest source of health coverage for Americans under 65, covering 165.6 million people, which makes employers central to any fix for women's health outcomes.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Employer benefit budgets are the main buyer channel for women's-health and fertility-benefit vendors in the US.
insights.locator: Why should we close the women's health gap?

insights.claim: 81% of human resources leaders say they are committed to advancing women's health, but only 52% of working women believe their benefits make healthcare affordable, a 29-point gap between employer intent and employee experience.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The gap between stated commitment and perceived affordability is room for vendors to win on redesigned benefits, and a retention risk for employers who do nothing.
insights.locator: Why should we close the women's health gap?

insights.claim: The authors argue that women's health lacks neither commitment nor investment but a system built around value, and that the $1 trillion a year from closing the women's health gap is a return that can be captured only through deliberate design.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Suggests capital should favor companies that change payment and benefit design, not those that simply add spending to the current system.
insights.quote: What's missing isn't commitment or investment — it's a system built around value.
insights.locator: Why should we close the women's health gap?
